paragraphs: Alyosha was heading across the cathedral square to the widow Morozov’s house, to see Grushenka. She had sent Fenya to him early that morning with an urgent message asking him to come. Fenya told him, when he questioned her, that her mistress had been particularly upset since the day before. In the two months since Mitya’s arrest, Alyosha had often visited the widow Morozov’s house, partly because he wished to and partly to carry messages for Mitya. Three days after Mitya was arrested, Grushenka had fallen gravely ill, and she remained ill for almost five weeks. For one whole week she had lain unconscious. She had changed a great deal. She was thinner and a little sallow, although for the last fortnight she had been well enough to go out. Yet to Alyosha her face was more attractive than ever, and he liked meeting her eyes when he came in. Her face had taken on a look of firmness and intelligent purpose. Something in her had been transformed inside, and one could see in her a quiet, fine, humble determination that nothing could shake. A small vertical line had appeared between her brows, and at first glance it gave her charming face a thoughtful, almost stern look. Hardly a trace remained of her old frivolity.

Alyosha found it strange, too, that the poor girl had not yet lost her youthful cheerfulness. A calamity had struck her: she was engaged to a man who was arrested for a terrible crime almost at the very moment of their engagement. She had been ill, and a sentence that seemed all but certain hung over Mitya. Even so, her cheerfulness had survived. Her once proud eyes now had a soft light in them, though now and then they blazed with the old vengeful fire, whenever one troubling thought gripped her harder than ever. What troubled her was the same as always: Katerina Ivanovna, whom Grushenka had even raved about in her delirium. Alyosha knew she was dreadfully jealous of her. And yet Katerina Ivanovna had not visited Mitya in prison even once, though she could have gone whenever she pleased. All this set Alyosha a hard problem, since he was the only person Grushenka confided in, and she kept asking him for advice. Sometimes he had nothing to tell her.

Anxious, he went into her rooms. She was at home. She had returned from visiting Mitya half an hour earlier, and the way she sprang up from her chair to meet him showed Alyosha she had been waiting for him with great impatience. On the table lay a pack of cards, dealt out for a game of “fools.” On the far side of the room a bed had been made up on the leather sofa, and Maximov lay on it, half sitting up. He wore a dressing-gown and a cotton nightcap. He was clearly ill and weak, but he was smiling happily. The homeless old man had come back from Mokroe with Grushenka two months earlier and had simply stayed, and he was still there. He had arrived with her in rain and sleet, sat down on the sofa soaked and frightened, and looked at her without a word, with a timid, imploring smile. Grushenka was in terrible grief and just coming down with fever. In everything she had to do in the first half-hour after she got home, she nearly forgot he was there. Then she happened to glance at him closely, and he gave a pitiful, helpless little laugh. She called Fenya and told her to give him something to eat. All that day he sat in the same spot, hardly moving. When it grew dark and the shutters were shut, Fenya asked her mistress:
“Is the gentleman staying the night, mistress?”
“Yes. Make up a bed for him on the sofa,” Grushenka answered.
She questioned him further and learned that he literally had nowhere to go. “Mr. Kalganov, my benefactor, told me flat out that he would not receive me again, and he gave me five roubles.”

“Well, God bless you, you’d better stay, then,” Grushenka decided, in her grief, and smiled at him with pity. Her smile wrung the old man’s heart, and his lips twitched with grateful tears. So the penniless wanderer had been with her ever since. He didn’t leave the house even while she was ill. Fenya and her grandmother, the cook, did not turn him out. They kept serving him his meals and making up his bed on the sofa. Grushenka had got used to him. When she came home from Mitya (she had started visiting him in prison before she was properly well), she would sit down and chat with “Maximushka” about small matters, so as not to think about her sorrow. The old man proved to be a good teller of stories now and then, and in the end she couldn’t do without him. Besides Alyosha, who did not come every day and never stayed long, Grushenka saw almost nobody. Her old merchant lay gravely ill at this time, “at his last gasp,” as people in town said, and in fact he died a week after Mitya’s trial. Three weeks before he died, sensing the end was near, he had at last made his sons, their wives and their children come upstairs to him, and he commanded them not to leave him again. From then on he gave his servants strict orders not to let Grushenka in, and to tell her, if she came, “The master wishes you long life and happiness and tells you to forget him.” Still, Grushenka sent almost every day to ask after him.

“You’ve come at last!” she cried, dropping the cards and welcoming Alyosha with delight. “Maximushka has been frightening me that you might not come. Ah, how much I need you! Sit down at the table. What will you have? Coffee?”
“Yes, please,” said Alyosha, taking his seat at the table. “I’m very hungry.”

“Good for you. Fenya, Fenya, coffee!” Grushenka cried. “It’s been ready for you for ages. And bring some little pies, and see they’re hot. Do you know, we had a storm over those pies today. I took them to the prison for him, and can you believe it, he threw them back at me. He wouldn’t eat them. He tossed one on the floor and stamped on it. So I told him, ‘I’m leaving them with the warder. If you haven’t eaten them by evening, your venomous spite must be all the food you need!’ And I walked out. Can you believe it, we quarreled again? Every time I go, we quarrel.”
Grushenka said all this in a single breath, upset as she was. Maximov grew nervous, smiled right away and looked down at the floor.
“What was the quarrel about this time?” Alyosha asked.

“I never saw it coming. Just think, he’s jealous of the Pole! ‘Why do you keep him?’ he said. ‘So now you’re keeping him.’ He’s jealous, jealous of me all the time, jealous when he’s eating, jealous when he’s asleep! Last week he even got it into his head to be jealous of Kuzma.”
“But he knew about the Pole already?”

“Yes, he did, but there you are. He has known about him from the very start, and today all at once he jumped up and began raging about him. I’m ashamed to repeat what he said. The silly fellow! Rakitin went in just as I was coming out. Maybe Rakitin is egging him on. What do you think?” she added, as if it hardly mattered.
“He loves you, that’s all it is. He loves you so much. And now he’s especially worried.”

“Well, he might be, with the trial tomorrow. And I went to him to say a word about tomorrow, because I’m afraid to think what will happen then. You say he’s worried, but how worried am I! And he goes on about the Pole! He’s too silly! At least he isn’t jealous of Maximushka yet.”
“My wife was terribly jealous over me, too,” Maximov put in a word.
“Jealous of you?” Grushenka couldn’t help laughing. “Who could she have been jealous of?”
“The servant girls.”

“Hush, Maximushka, I’m not in a laughing mood now. I’m angry. Stop eyeing the pies. You’re not getting any. They’re bad for you, and I won’t give you vodka either. I have to look after him as well, as if I were running an almshouse,” she laughed.
“I don’t deserve your kindness. I’m a worthless creature,” said Maximov, tears in his voice. “You’d do better to spend your kindness on people who are more use than I am.”

“Ech, everybody is of use, Maximushka, and who can say who’s most useful? If only that Pole didn’t exist, Alyosha. He’s gone and fallen ill today, too. I’ve been to see him as well. And I’ll send him some pies, too, on purpose. I hadn’t sent him any, but Mitya accused me of it, so now I will! Ah, here comes Fenya with a letter! Yes, it’s from the Poles—begging again!”

Pan Mussyalovitch had indeed sent a very long letter, eloquent in his usual way, begging her to lend him three roubles. A receipt for the sum was enclosed, with a promise to repay it within three months, signed by Pan Vrublevsky as well. Over the fortnight of her recovery Grushenka had received many such letters from her former lover, each with a receipt like this. She knew, though, that the two Poles had called to ask about her health while she was ill. The first letter they sent her was a long one, written on large notepaper and sealed with a big family crest. It was so obscure and high-flown that Grushenka put it down before she was halfway through, unable to make anything of it. She was in no state to deal with letters then. Next day a second letter followed the first, in which Pan Mussyalovitch asked her for a loan of two thousand roubles, for a very short time. Grushenka left that one unanswered too. Then came a whole series of letters, one a day, all just as pompous and rhetorical, but the sum they asked for kept shrinking. It fell to a hundred roubles, then twenty-five, then ten, and at last Grushenka got a letter in which both Poles begged for only one rouble and enclosed a receipt signed by the two of them.

Then Grushenka suddenly felt sorry for them, and at dusk she went to their lodging herself. She found the two Poles in great poverty, almost starving, with no food or firewood, without even cigarettes, and in debt to their landlady. The two hundred roubles they had carried off from Mitya at Mokroe had soon vanished. But Grushenka was surprised to be received with haughty dignity and self-importance, with the most elaborate manners and pompous speeches. Grushenka simply laughed and gave her old admirer ten roubles. Then she told Mitya about it, laughing, and he wasn’t in the least jealous. But from that day the Poles had fastened on Grushenka and bombarded her daily with demands for money, and she had always sent them small sums. And now, today of all days, Mitya had taken it into his head to be fearfully jealous.

“Like a fool, I stopped by to see him for just a minute on my way to Mitya’s, because he’s ill too, my Pole,” Grushenka began again, in a nervous rush. “I was laughing as I told Mitya about it. ‘Just think,’ I said, ‘my Pole had the happy idea of singing me his old songs, with a guitar. He thought I’d be touched and marry him!’ Mitya jumped up, swearing.... Well, there you are, I’ll send them the pies! Fenya, is it that little girl they’ve sent? Here, give her three roubles, wrap a dozen pies up in paper and tell her to take them. And you, Alyosha, be sure to tell Mitya that I did send them the pies.”
